evidence_quotes.quote: This study is based on ethnographic research I carried out in the San Quint´ın Valley in the summers of 2005, 2006, and 2009.

I attended community meetings that addressed the chronic shortage of water in these and other colonias—rural squatter settlements where farm laborers built their homes and interviewed residents who have participated in collective mobilizations for water. I also interviewed public ofﬁcials, heads of water agencies, and representatives of growers’ associations to gather their perspectives on the water problems in the region.

The agency has only 32 urban wells (some of which are dry), signiﬁcantly fewer than the wells registered for irrigation; about 40 percent of the colonias in the region do not have running water. Some of the oldest squatter settlements waited many years before CESPE built the infrastructure to deliver water, while in the colonias with no running water, residents have to buy it at inﬂated prices from private vendors in water trucks.

Responding to the new Mexican water law, state politicians increased the cost of piped water to make the agency ﬁnancially sustainable. At ﬁrst, CESPE proposed an increase of about 300 percent to take effect in 2007, but massive protests by residents, merchants, and small business owners derailed the plan. For residents who did not have meters and paid a ﬂat fee, the cost of water increased 115 percent (from Mex$23 to Mex$53 per month).

To hold residents accountable, CESPE started to install water meters, the installation of which was heavily subsidized for agrarian wells. For households, however, the average cost for installing a meter was $227 (around Mex$2,500), well beyond the limited means of most farm laborer families.

Each new contract came with three separate fees: a connection fee, a piping fee, and the water meter. In contrast, unlike domestic users, growers do not pay the government of the municipality for the use of water.

After several years of public pressure, CESPE ﬁnally started to deliver water in its own trucks at a lower price than private vendors. Yet because of its own limited supplies, it set up a quota of ﬁve barrels per week per household, regardless of its size, well below the amount of water most of the families in the colonia used.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines domestic household and settlement-level drinking and household water service access in rural squatter settlements (colonias, including Colonia Arbolitos) in the San Quintin Valley, Baja California, delivered via the state public water utility CESPE (piped water connections and utility water trucks) and private water vendors.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines national and state water governance, utility management, and regulatory policies (1992 National Water Law decentralization, CNA agricultural regulation, and CESPE urban/domestic water provision). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, rather than treating neoliberalism merely as unanalysed macro-governance background, the paper empirically analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing domestic water service access: (1) tariff and full cost-recovery rules enacted by CESPE under the 1992 National Water Law (a proposed 300% hike and enacted 115% flat-fee increase from Mex$23 to Mex$53/month, rounded up per federal fee-rounding law, plus phased 50%/50%/40% hikes); (2) mandatory household metering and three-part new-contract charges (connection fee, piping fee, and unsubsidized $227 / Mex$2,500 water meter cost, contrasted with 75% meter subsidies and zero municipal water charges for agricultural wells); (3) administrative rationing/allocation rules (CESPE's uniform quota of five barrels per week per household regardless of family size for trucked water delivery); and (4) weak CNA enforcement of groundwater well-permitting bans and grower capture of statutory watershed councils (COTAS).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical qualitative socio-legal / ethnographic field study conducted across the summers of 2005, 2006, and 2009, combining participant observation in two rural settlements and community meetings, semi-structured interviews in 18 farmworker households, interviews with mobilized residents, and key-informant interviews with public officials, water agency heads (CESPE, SAGARPA), and grower association / COTAS representatives. Per protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review and mechanism synthesis without quantitative effect estimates.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access, connection, continuity, quantity, quality, and affordability outcomes: roughly 40% of colonias lack running water; multi-year delays before piped connection in Colonia Arbolitos; intermittent piped service (e.g., three days a week for a few hours at night); rationing below household need under CESPE's five-barrel weekly quota; household water expenditures of ~14% of farmworker income (Mex$300/month) before piped connection vs. Mex$40/month after connection (with unsubsidized $227 meter fees beyond household means); and degraded water quality (salinity and unfiltered muddy tap water) requiring private purchase of drinking/cooking water.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (indigenous Mixtec/Zapotec and mestizo farmworker households and rural colonias in the San Quintin Valley, plus regional water agencies), exposure (CESPE cost-recovery tariffs, connection/piping/meter fees, five-barrel household quota, and asymmetric CNA regulatory enforcement/subsidies under the 1992 National Water Law), outcomes (piped coverage, continuity, quantity, affordability, and reliance on private vendors), and study design (ethnographic case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Qualitative ethnographic case study (participant observation and semi-structured household and key-informant interviews)
population_and_sample: Indigenous (Mixtec, Zapotec, Triqui) and mestizo farmworker households and rural squatter settlements (colonias, including Colonia Arbolitos) in the San Quintin Valley, Baja California, Mexico, alongside regional water agencies and grower bodies (participant observation in 2 rural settlements and community meetings, semi-structured interviews in 18 households, and interviews with public officials, water agency heads, and grower association representatives across summers 2005, 2006, and 2009).
exposure: Water governance, tariff/cost-recovery, metering/connection-fee, quota, and regulatory enforcement rules under Mexico's 1992 National Water Law—specifically state utility (CESPE) full cost-recovery tariff increases (115% flat-fee hike), three-part new-contract charges (connection, piping, and unsubsidized $227 household meter fees), CESPE's uniform 5-barrel-per-week household trucked-water quota, and asymmetric federal agricultural subsidies and weak CNA groundwater well-permitting enforcement.
outcome: Household and settlement-level domestic water service access, including piped running-water connection coverage (~40% of colonias unconnected), service continuity and rationing (intermittent cuts to 3 days/week for a few hours at night; 5-barrel weekly trucked quota vs. 10-barrel household need), affordability and household water expenditure (~14% of income pre-connection vs. Mex$40/month post-connection; unaffordable $227 meter fee; forced reliance on higher-priced private truck vendors), and delivered water quality (salinity and unfiltered mud).
rationale: This English-language ethnographic study satisfies all inclusion criteria (c1–c6) for the systematic review. Based on multi-year fieldwork (2005, 2006, 2009) including 18 semi-structured household interviews, participant observation in two rural colonias, and official/utility interviews in Baja California, Mexico, it examines household and settlement-level domestic water service access provided by the state water utility CESPE. Beyond macro-level political-economy framing, it directly investigates concrete rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing domestic service access under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification—including CESPE's cost-recovery tariff increases under the 1992 National Water Law, three-part household connection/piping/meter contract fees ($227 unsubsidized meter cost), CESPE's five-barrel-per-week household trucked-water quota rule, and weak CNA enforcement of agricultural well-permitting rules—and documents their effects on household connection, continuity, quantity, and affordability. Per review rules, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are included for mechanism synthesis regardless of lacking quantitative effect sizes.
